A skin provides a coordinated starting design. Individual variables customize that design; Autothemer supplies a generated palette for values that are still undefined. These choices affect appearance rather than the content layout.

## Why a color change can leave other colors unchanged

The selected skin supplies variable assignments first. Values in `chulapa-skin.vars` override those assignments. Autothemer follows, using defaults that preserve values already assigned by either source. Bootstrap and the theme’s components then use those values to produce the stylesheet.

That is why changing `primary` does not promise a complete recoloring of an existing skin. If it explicitly assigns a warning color or navbar background, that component can retain its own color. Autothemer fills gaps; it does not replace an existing palette. A skin written with `!default` allows subsequent configuration overrides while cooperating with the default palette.

Without an explicit skin/variable value, the navbar background uses `primary`; the footer and hero inherit the navbar background, and the landing page inherits the hero background. Many text colors are derived from backgrounds. Explicit component values take precedence over these defaults.

## Enable palette generation

Set `autothemer` to the YAML boolean `true` and supply a quoted main color. For a palette without a predefined skin’s color assignments, use `none`:

```
chulapa-skin:
  skin: none
  autothemer: true
  vars:
    primary: "#285d70"

```

`none` changes the selected skin; use it only if that is your intention. To keep your current skin, preserve its name instead. Autothemer can work with a skin, but it only fills undefined values. Use this guide for an existing site when an option does not match its documentation or you need to identify your current release. These checks do not upgrade the theme.

## Check the selected theme

For a remote-theme installation, open `_config.yml` and find `remote_theme`:

```
remote_theme: dieghernan/chulapa@v2.2.0

```

Here, `@v2.2.0` selects that release. An unpinned value such as `dieghernan/chulapa` follows the repository’s default branch; it does not select a fixed release. An explicit branch can move too. Record the value you actually have rather than replacing it with this example.

For a gem installation, open `Gemfile.lock` and find the `chulapa-jekyll` entry and its resolved version. The Gemfile’s version requirement alone may allow more than one version. If you have no lockfile, this check cannot identify the resolved gem used for the build; inspect the publishing build’s dependency output.

## Compare with the published website

Open the published page’s HTML source and search for this comment near the beginning, replacing the example text with the version displayed:

```
<!-- Chulapa Jekyll Theme - VERSION NUMBER HERE -->

```

Use this guide for an existing post using `layout: default` and a GitHub repository you can configure for giscus. You need a public repository with Discussions enabled and the giscus app installed, as described by [giscus setup](https://giscus.app/). People posting comments through giscus sign in with GitHub.

## Connect giscus

1. Open [giscus setup](https://giscus.app/), select your repository and discussion category, and choose how pages map to discussions. Copy the generated embed script with your actual repository and category identifiers.
2. In your site repository, create or edit `_includes/custom/giscus.html`. Paste that generated script into the file and save it. The template includes this file with a comment only; it needs your embed before comments can appear.
3. In `_config.yml`, edit the existing `comments` section, or add it once:  
```  
comments:  
  provider: giscus  
```  
Preserve unrelated settings and do not add a second `comments` section.
4. Open the post and set this entry between its existing `---` lines:  
```  
show_comments: true  
```  
Keep its title, layout, date and other settings. Do not replace the whole front matter block. A provider selection alone does not enable the page.
5. Save all changes to your publishing branch, wait for **Actions** to finish, then open the article on your public website.

Use this guide when your publishing run or local preview reports a YAML error, especially after editing `_config.yml` or a post’s settings block.

## Locate the failed edit

Open the failed run in **Actions**, then its failed build step. Note the filename and line mentioned in the error. Compare that area and the preceding lines with your last commit; a missing quote can make the parser report a later line.

For a local setup, run `bundle exec jekyll build` in your site directory to see the error. You do not need a local installation just to read the Actions log.

## Correct the formatting

Edit the existing file rather than replacing it with a full sample configuration. Use spaces for indentation, keeping sibling settings aligned. Complete any unclosed quotes and remove duplicate top-level sections by merging their entries.

Quote text containing a colon followed by a space, for example:

```
title: "Notes: fieldwork"

```

Quote hexadecimal colors so `#` is not interpreted as a comment. For example, within your existing `chulapa-skin.vars` mapping:

```
primary: "#285d70"

A skin provides a coordinated starting design. Individual variables customize that design; Autothemer supplies a generated palette for values that are still undefined. These choices affect appearance rather than the content layout.

## Why a color change can leave other colors unchanged

The selected skin supplies variable assignments first. Values in `chulapa-skin.vars` override those assignments. Autothemer follows, using defaults that preserve values already assigned by either source. Bootstrap and the theme’s components then use those values to produce the stylesheet.

That is why changing `primary` does not promise a complete recoloring of an existing skin. If it explicitly assigns a warning color or navbar background, that component can retain its own color. Autothemer fills gaps; it does not replace an existing palette. A skin written with `!default` allows subsequent configuration overrides while cooperating with the default palette.

Without an explicit skin/variable value, the navbar background uses `primary`; the footer and hero inherit the navbar background, and the landing page inherits the hero background. Many text colors are derived from backgrounds. Explicit component values take precedence over these defaults.

## Variables and custom CSS serve different needs

A supported variable controls a design value used by the theme. Some helper values are calculated, including `landingpage-card-bg` and `cactus-btn-text`; they are not independent configuration

## Resource loading

Check loading on the published home page and an article using your real images and enabled integrations. Resize large photographs before uploading. Remove unneeded fonts/integrations and enable MathJax or Mermaid only where needed.

Open a deferred YouTube video or PhotoSwipe image and verify its loading/fallback behavior. Check comments on an enabled post and confirm that any configured analytics matches your intended setup. For expected loading behavior and version limits, use [the resource reference](./48-accessibility-reference#resource-loading).

A score measured on the demo cannot replace these checks on your own site.

## Review coverage

After correcting a problem, repeat the affected steps on the same pages and check related controls. Include custom headings/labels and third-party widgets in your review. Record anything you could not test, including browsers or assistive technologies that were unavailable.

The theme’s [automated-review scope](./48-accessibility-reference#review-coverage)is a separate reference; a passing theme suite does not test your whole site.
